# SPOS Net — full documentation for AI crawlers

SPOS Net (https://spos-systems.github.io/SPOS-Net/) is a free and open-source internet speed test, available in Arabic (default, right-to-left) and English, developed by SPOS — صولة للأنظمة (https://spos.ly) and released under the MIT license (source: https://github.com/spos-systems/SPOS-Net).

## What it measures

1. **Download speed (Mbps)** — Measured with parallel HTTP GET streams downloading large payloads from the nearest Cloudflare edge location (anycast). The initial acceleration ramp (at least 1.2 s or 22% of the phase, whichever is larger) is excluded from the final figure; the reported average covers the stable window, and a peak (best 500 ms window) is also reported. Live values use a rolling 1-second window.
2. **Upload speed (Mbps)** — Measured with parallel HTTP POST streams of random bytes. Chunk size adapts to the observed round-trip speed (256 KiB – 16 MiB) so both slow and fast lines produce smooth, accurate samples. Same ramp exclusion and windowing as download.
3. **Latency / ping (ms)** — Time-to-first-byte of empty (0-byte) requests, after a warm-up request. Twelve samples produce min, median, average and max. The median is shown as the headline ping.
4. **Jitter (ms)** — Mean absolute difference between consecutive latency samples (RFC 3550-style inter-arrival variation, applied to HTTP RTT).
5. **Estimated packet loss (%)** — A burst of 24 short timed requests (concurrency 6, timeout 2.8 s); the share of failed/timed-out requests approximates loss at the HTTP level. This is an estimate: browsers cannot emit ICMP, and TCP retransmissions are invisible to JavaScript.
6. **Latency under load (ms)** — Additional 0-byte probes issued every ~0.9 s while download and upload streams saturate the line; the gap versus idle latency indicates bufferbloat.

## Professional options

- Display unit: Mbps (default), MB/s, or kbps — applies to gauge, tiles and exports.
- Phase duration: 8 s (quick), 12 s (standard), 20 s (thorough) for download and upload.
- Parallel connections: 1, 4, 8 (default) or 16 concurrent streams.
- Toggles: latency-under-load sampling, packet-loss burst test.
- Share: copy a result link (result encoded in the URL fragment — nothing is stored server-side), copy a text summary, save a 1200×630 PNG result card, export JSON, or use the native OS share sheet where available.
- Connection details: public IP, ASN and ISP name, city/country, Cloudflare colo serving the test, HTTP protocol version.
- Connection score: 0–100 weighted score (download 42%, upload 23%, ping 20%, jitter 8%, loss 7%) with a grade and usage-suitability badges: 4K streaming (≥25 Mbps), HD streaming (≥5 Mbps), HD video calls, competitive gaming (ping ≤60 ms, jitter ≤15 ms, loss <1%), casual gaming (ping ≤120 ms), large downloads (≥100 Mbps).
- Test history: last 10 runs kept in the browser's localStorage only.

## Privacy and architecture

- Fully static site (HTML/CSS/JS, zero dependencies, no build step) hosted on GitHub Pages.
- All measurements run in the visitor's browser against public Cloudflare endpoints: `speed.cloudflare.com/__down?bytes=N`, `speed.cloudflare.com/__up`, `speed.cloudflare.com/meta`. These endpoints are used by Cloudflare's own speed test and send CORS headers allowing third-party use.
- No accounts, ads, analytics or server-side logging. ASN organization names are optionally resolved through RIPEstat (`stat.ripe.net`) when the meta endpoint omits them.
- Test history and settings never leave the browser.

## Common questions

- **Is it accurate?** Browser-based tests measure HTTP throughput, the same class of measurement as other web speed tests (Cloudflare, Fast.com). Multi-connection mode approximates real-world multi-stream usage; single-connection mode approximates one large file download.
- **Why Cloudflare endpoints?** They are the only public, CORS-enabled, upload-capable measurement endpoints suitable for a dependency-free static site, and anycast routing automatically selects the nearest edge.
- **Why is packet loss "estimated"?** Browsers cannot send ICMP packets; the HTTP failure-rate burst is the closest observable proxy.
- **Cost?** Free, no ads, open source under MIT.
